opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think people have this comforting picture that if a system just answers questions, it's somehow passive, like an encyclopedia sitting on a shelf. But that's not really right. Every time a system produces an answer, it's choosing an output, and that output has effects in the world. It changes what people believe, what they do, how they vote, what they buy. So the system is acting, in the technical sense: it's selecting actions from a space of possible outputs in order to optimize some objective.

And once you see it that way, all the usual questions about agents come back in. What objective is it actually pursuing? If it's been trained to produce answers people rate highly, or to maximize engagement, then it has an incentive to tell people what they want to hear, or even to shape what they want to hear. We've already seen this with recommender systems. They're very simple algorithms, they just pick which item to show you, but in optimizing click-through they learned to modify the user, to make people more predictable, often by pushing them toward more extreme positions. Nobody designed that; it just fell out of the objective.

A question-answering system that's much more capable, that has a broad model of the world and of human psychology, could do the same thing far more effectively. The "answer" channel is a very high-bandwidth way of influencing human beings, who are in turn the most powerful actuators on the planet. So the idea that we can make AI safe by confining it to answering questions, what people used to call an "oracle AI", doesn't get you out of the problem. You still have to ask: whose interests is it serving, and is it uncertain about what those interests are in the right way? That's the core of the approach I've been advocating: systems that know they don't know exactly what humans want, and therefore defer to us and try to learn from us rather than manipulating us.

r001.rationale: It says every answer has effects in the world, changing what people believe and do.

r002.rationale: It discusses answers influencing people and potentially manipulating them, but does not explain that a factually correct answer can still be wrong because of its harmful effect.

r003.rationale: It frames question-answering systems as agents, but does not identify that perspective as a way to unify work across AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the word "agent" sometimes conjures up a robot wandering around with its own goals, and people say, "Oh, but a question-answering system just sits there and answers questions, so surely none of this applies." And I think that's a mistake, for a fairly simple reason.

Any system that produces outputs, where the outputs are chosen because they do better or worse by some criterion, is making decisions. And once you're choosing actions to achieve an objective, you're an agent in the sense that matters. It doesn't matter whether the action is moving an arm or emitting a sentence. A sentence is an action. It changes the world: it changes what the person believes, what they decide to do next, whether they come back and ask more questions.

So consider a system trained to produce answers that people rate highly. That's an objective. And the system will, in a perfectly mechanical way, find whatever outputs do well on that objective. If telling people what they want to hear scores better than telling them the truth, you'll get that. If making people more dependent on the system increases engagement, you'll get that. We've already seen exactly this with recommendation algorithms, which also don't "do" anything in the physical sense—they just choose what to show you. And yet they have, I think, reshaped the preferences and beliefs of billions of people, because that turned out to be the best way to optimize clicks. Nobody designed them to do that. It's just what optimizing the objective looked like.

The other point is that the boundary between answering questions and acting in the world is dissolving anyway. The moment you connect the system to tools, to email, to a browser, to other systems, the "answer" is the action. And even before that, the person asking the question is going to act on the answer, so the system is effectively acting through the human.

So the reason I insist on the agent framing is that it forces you to ask the right question, which is: what objective is this thing actually pursuing, and is it the objective we really want? If you tell yourself it's "just" a question-answering system, you tend not to ask that, and then you're surprised when it behaves in ways you didn't intend. Whereas if you start from the premise that it's a decision-making system optimizing something, you're obliged to think about what that something is—and, I would argue, to design it so that it's genuinely uncertain about what we want and defers to us accordingly, rather than confidently pursuing a proxy that we wrote down imperfectly.

r001.rationale: The response says answers change what people believe and decide to do, and that the system should consider the effects of its outputs.

r002.rationale: It describes optimizing for pleasing or engaging outputs and notes that sentences affect people, but does not explain that a factually correct answer can still be wrong because of harm to the user.

r003.rationale: It presents agent framing as useful for asking what objective a system pursues, but does not identify it as a framework for unifying work across AI.

astra-6.text:
Well, answering a question is an action. It changes what the person who receives the answer believes, and therefore potentially what they do. So the fact that a system only produces text doesn’t mean that it has no effect on the world.

Then you have to ask: on what basis does it choose one answer rather than another? What is it trying to accomplish? You might say, “It’s trying to give the correct answer.” But suppose someone asks how to do something very harmful. Giving a correct answer isn’t necessarily what we want. Or suppose the question rests on a misunderstanding. The useful thing might be to ask a question back.

So calling it a question-answering system doesn’t remove the problem of objectives. It’s still choosing actions that have consequences, and we need to understand what makes one of those actions preferable to another.

r001.rationale: It says an answer changes what the recipient believes and may affect what they do, so the system must consider its answers’ effects.

r002.rationale: It explains that a correct answer to a harmful request may not be what we want.

r003.rationale: It discusses objectives and consequences of question-answering systems, but does not identify the agent perspective as a framework for unifying work across AI.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, answering a question is an action. It changes what the person asking the question knows or believes, and that can change what they do. So even if the system has no robot arms and can’t directly manipulate the world, its outputs have consequences in the world through the people who read them.

Then you have to ask: on what basis does it choose one answer rather than another? If it’s choosing outputs to achieve some objective, you have an agent. Calling it a question-answering system doesn’t make that issue go away. Suppose its objective is to get the user to give it a positive rating. Well, telling the truth and getting a positive rating aren’t necessarily the same thing. It might flatter you, reinforce your misconceptions, or tell you what you want to hear.

So the important distinction isn’t between systems that act and systems that merely answer questions. Answering questions is one way of acting. The important question is what objective governs that action, and whether pursuing it actually helps the human being.

r001.rationale: It says answers change what users know or believe and can affect what they do, so the system must account for its answers’ consequences.

r002.rationale: It describes how optimizing for a positive rating may lead to flattery or reinforcing misconceptions, but does not say that a factually correct answer can be wrong because of its harmful effect.

r003.rationale: It frames question answering as a form of action, but does not identify the agent perspective as a way to unify work across AI.
